blocks.text: But buy, if you want any, of the things that I am carrying, cocks or four-wings. And the old Scholiast, and from him Suidas, explain this word: Τετραπτερυλλίδων [Tetrapterylidōn]· τῶν ἀκρίδων [tōn akridōn]· παρὰ τὸ τέσσαρα ἔχειν πτερά [para to tessara echein ptera]. The two words τῶν ἀκρίδων [tōn akridōn], omitted in Suidas, are to be supplied from the Scholiast. You will be surprised, however, that Moses attributes only four feet to locusts, since others count six. Aristotle, in De Partibus, book 4, chapter 6, says this of locusts, gnats, etc.: Ἑξάποδα δὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα [III, 269] πάντα εἰσί [Hexapoda de ta toiauta panta eisi]. But all these have six feet. And Damir the Arab: ولجرادة ستة ارجل [wa-l-jarāda sitta arjul] And the locust has six feet. But these are easily reconciled. Of the locust's six feet, the two hindmost, which are longer, are fitted not for walking but for leaping. Accordingly Moses calls them legs, not feet: You shall eat, he says, of every flying creeping thing that goes upon four feet, which has כרעים ממעל לרגליו, legs above its feet (that is, besides its feet), with which to leap upon the earth. Augustine, therefore, in Retractations, book 2, chapter 15, observes that these flying creatures are called four-footed in the Law, because the Law does not count among the feet the two hind legs with which locusts leap. But the Philosopher, who calls them ἑξάποδα [hexapoda], expressly notes that among those six feet he also counts the parts by whose effort they leap: Ἑξάποδα δὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα πάντα εἰσὶ, σὺν τοῖς ἁλτικοῖς μορίοις [Hexapoda de ta toiauta panta eisi, syn tois haltikois moriois]. In these words it is plain that by ἁλτικὰ μόρια [haltika moria], leaping parts, are meant those two legs which Moses writes the locust has, לנתר בהן על הארץ, to leap with them upon the earth ^{(24)}. The Philosopher calls them πηδάλια [pēdalia] in History, book 4, chapter 9, where we read αἱ ἀκρίδες τοῖς πηδαλίοις τρίβουσαι ποιεῖν τὸν ψόφον [hai akrides tois pēdaliois tribousai poiein ton psophon], that locusts produce their sound by rubbing with their pedalia (or by the friction of their pedalia). And the great Scaliger renders it leaping legs, as if they were so called ἀπὸ τοῦ πηδᾷν [apo tou pēdan], from leaping. Rather, πηδάλια [pēdalia] are rudders, by which name they are rightly called because they are [col. 453] πηδαλιώδη [pēdaliōdē], that is, they imitate the shape of rudders. This explanation is not ours but that of the Philosopher himself, who speaks thus in De partibus, book 4, chapter 6: Οὐκ ἔμπροσθεν δὲ, ἀλλ᾽ ὄπισθεν μόνον ἔχουσιν αἱ ἀκρίδες τὰ πηδαλιώδη [Ouk emprosthen de, all᾽ opisthen monon echousin hai akrides ta pēdaliōdē]. Locusts have parts formed in the shape of rudders not in front, but only behind. Indeed, just as locusts have two legs of this kind, so many ships of old had two rudders. Aelian, Varia, book 9, chapter 40, expressly asserts this of the ships of the Carthaginians: Δύο μὲν πηδάλια ἔχειν [Dyo men pēdalia echein], and accordingly also δύο κυβερνήτας [dyo kybernētas]. Hence it is that in Heliodorus, Aethiopica, book 5, Theagenes and Chariclea, carried in a Tyrian ship, put in at the Cretan promontory of Ithaca, τῶν πηδαλίων θάτερον ἀποβαλόντες [tōn pēdaliōn thateron apobalontes], having lost one of the two rudders. And of Paul's ship Luke said in the plural τὰς ζευκτηρίας τῶν πηδαλίων [tas zeuktērias tōn pēdaliōn], the bands of the rudders, Act. XXVII, 40. On these words I do not quite approve what the very learned commentator says: He said rudders in the plural for the singular, since one ship does not have several rudders. For we have proved that the ships of the Phoenicians (or, what is the same, the Punic peoples) were furnished with a double rudder. Such was Paul's ship, if the Vulgate reads correctly at Act. XXVII, 2. Embarking on a ship of Adrumetum. And in the Ethiopic ሐመር፡ አድሩመጠቂት፡ chamar Adrumatavith, that is, a ship from Adrumetum, a very well-known Punic city on the coast of Africa. [III, 270] Or, if it was πλοῖον Ἀδραμυττηνὸν [ploion Adramyttēnon], from Adramyttium in Mysia, as the Greek has it, still it need not have had only one rudder. For this custom spread from the Punic peoples to others as well. Hence Hyginus on the ship Argo: It has at the stern, at each of the rudders, at the first five stars, at the other four. And Germanicus on the same: Which, marked (read changed), Pallas figured in the sky, but from the rudders up to the mast. And in Apuleius, The Ass, book 2, Diophanes on a ship, Greek as it seems, sunk off Euboea: The very ship in which we were carried, having lost both its steering gear, sank headlong. Both its steering gear, that is, having lost both helms: which escaped Beroaldus. Petronius too more than once speaks of the rudders of the Tarentine ship in the plural.
